summary: Summarizes issues around the routing and addressing scaling problems in the IP architecture and gives background on the ROAD group and related activities in the IETF. It is informational.

eli5.summary: The Internet's address lists were growing too long for routers and addresses were running out. This paper tells what a group was doing about it.

subtitle: An IESG analysis of Internet scaling problems and the ROAD group's recommended solutions.

tldr.problem: Rapid Internet growth in the early 1990s was creating three acute problems: rapid exhaustion of Class B IP address blocks, explosion in the size of routing tables, and eventual depletion of the entire IPv4 address space.
tldr.mechanism: The IESG and the ROAD (Routing and Addressing) group analyzed these problems and proposed a phased approach: immediate operational improvements, short-term fixes like CIDR for routing aggregation, mid-term exploration of larger address spaces, and long-term Internet layer evolution.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends adopting CIDR immediately for routing table relief and Class B conservation, while pursuing multiple proposals for bigger addresses. This set the foundation for IPv6 development.

today: RFC 1380 is an Informational RFC documenting a pivotal moment in Internet history. The IESG's phased approach proved prescient: CIDR was successfully deployed and extended IPv4's lifetime, while IPv6 development proceeded according to criteria outlined here. The address exhaustion problem was eventually addressed through IPv6's 128-bit address space.

sections.title: The Internet Growth Crisis
sections.content:
By 1992, explosive Internet growth had begun straining its foundational architecture. The Internet was no longer limited to research institutions; it extended to businesses, schools, and homes worldwide. This unprecedented success exposed three interrelated scaling problems that threatened Internet growth. The Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) convened the ROAD group (Routing and Addressing) to analyze these problems and recommend solutions. This RFC summarizes those findings and proposes a strategy for the IETF.

The problems were pressing and required action on multiple time horizons simultaneously: immediate operational fixes, short-term protocol improvements, medium-term address space expansion, and long-term architectural enhancements.
sections.eli5: The Internet was growing super fast, and this was breaking things. A group of engineers had to figure out how to fix it without breaking what was already working.

sections.title: The Three Scaling Problems
sections.content:
Class B Exhaustion: IP addresses were allocated in three classes. Class B blocks held enough addresses for medium-sized networks and were quickly running out. At the current allocation rate, all unassigned Class B numbers would be exhausted in less than two years. After that, new sites would need multiple Class C blocks, making routing worse.

Routing Table Explosion: As more networks connected to the Internet, routing tables grew exponentially. Routers had memory limits and could store only a finite number of routes. Some routers were already unable to handle the full table. Network operators faced growing burden of manually configuring routing policies, and routing protocols (like EGP and RIP) designed for small networks consumed significant bandwidth.

IP Address Exhaustion: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, providing about 4 billion possible addresses. With exponential growth, eventually the entire space could be exhausted, forcing a fundamental protocol change.
sections.eli5: Three things were happening at once: the address blocks for medium-sized networks were running out, routers had too many networks to track, and eventually all possible addresses would be used up.

sections.title: Proposed Solutions and Trade-Offs
sections.content:
For Class B exhaustion, solutions include: reclaim unused addresses, tighten allocation policies, or use aggregation schemes like CIDR to create custom-sized blocks from Class C space.

For routing table explosion, solutions vary by cause. Hardware limitations can be addressed by deploying powerful routers or offloading computation to servers. Human limits require better tools. Long-term, routing aggregation offers the best solution: hierarchical address assignment allows multiple routes to summarize as a single entry, reducing table size.

For IP address exhaustion, proposals range from larger address spaces (a new protocol) to address translation (where hosts use private addresses) to partitioned Internets where addresses are unique only within an area. Each approach carries significant costs in implementation and transition effort.
sections.eli5: For running out of middle-sized blocks: use smaller ones and group them. For routing becoming too big: build faster routers or summarize routes. For running out of addresses: make addresses much bigger, reuse them locally, or split the Internet into regions.

sections.title: The ROAD Group and IESG Recommendations
sections.content:
The ROAD group, formed at the November 1991 IETF, brought together IAB and BGP working group participants to explore near-term solutions. The group concluded that CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) was the best immediate approach. CIDR allows address blocks of arbitrary size and enables route aggregation, providing relief on both Class B exhaustion and routing table explosion.

The IESG proposed a phased approach. The immediate phase includes operational actions like conservative address allocation and topology design. The short-term phase focuses on deploying CIDR and updating routing protocols like BGP. The mid-term phase addresses IP address exhaustion through a major protocol change. The long-term phase anticipates Internet layer evolution with quality-of-service support and resource reservation.

The RFC establishes formal criteria for evaluating bigger address space proposals, including deployment plan, security impact, backward compatibility, and performance. Working groups would be formed for each proposal.
sections.eli5: The ROAD group decided to use CIDR right away to help with the two smaller problems. For the big problem of running out of addresses, they set up a formal process to study different ideas and pick the best.

sections.title: CIDR and Immediate Actions
sections.content:
The IESG strongly endorsed CIDR as the solution for short-term crisis. CIDR requires three components: a plan for hierarchical address assignment, classless routing protocols that carry address masks, and deployment guidelines. Unlike larger address space proposals, CIDR requires no changes to host software, only to routers and routing protocols.

Beyond CIDR, the IESG endorsed immediate actions needing no protocol changes: conservative allocation policies, reclamation of unused Class B addresses, installation of powerful routers at key points, and careful topology design. While these cannot solve fundamental problems, they slow their onset and buy time for longer-term solutions.
sections.eli5: CIDR was the chosen fix: routers could group addresses without changing how programs talk to the Internet. Some things could start immediately: be careful with addresses, upgrade routers, and design networks smarter.

items.title: Class B Exhaustion
items.text: Medium blocks running out in ~2 years.

items.title: Routing Explosion
items.text: Too many routes for router memory.
